b: Structured programming is a technique for writing clear, logical code that is easy to read, understand, debug and maintain. C++, C and Java support it.
Programs run instruction by instruction with no random jumping. This is why structured programming is almost synonymous with eliminating GOTO.
C++ gives four control flow concepts: sequence, selection, repetition and subroutine statements.

q.q: Structured programming is almost synonymous with…
Which is NOT one of the four control flow concepts?
q.e: The four are sequence, selection, repetition and subroutine.

b: Sequence structure means statements run one after the other, in the order they are written.
Example: int a = 5; int b = 6; int c = a * b; cout << c; This sets a to 5, b to 6, stores the product 30 in c, then displays it.
In a flow chart, a rectangle is a statement and an arrow is the flow to the next one.

q.q: In a sequence structure, statements run…
q.e: Each statement starts after the previous one finishes.

q.q: After int a = 5; int b = 6; int c = a * b; what does c hold?

b: Selection statements use a Boolean expression that is true or false to decide what runs next.
if (condition) { ... } runs the block only when the condition is true, and skips it when false.
if ... else runs one block when true and a different block when false. Afterwards, execution continues with the statement after the else block.
Example: if (age >= 18) { calculate pay } else { print that the person is under age }.

q.q: An if single-selection statement does what when the condition is false?
q.e: Without an else, nothing in the block runs.

o: A different action for true and for false
q.e: One block for true, another for false.

b: A nested if is an if or if...else placed inside another one. There is no limit to nesting.
Nested if...else chains handle multiple alternatives. Example: if (score >= 70) grade = 'A'; else if (score >= 60) grade = 'B'; and so on down to else grade = 'F'.
When several conditions are true, only the first matching branch runs. Order your conditions from highest to lowest.

q.q: In an else-if chain, if several conditions are true, how many branches run?
q.e: After the first match, the rest are skipped.
The inner if only runs when the outer condition passes.
